summary: ASTRAMED is an on-board astronaut health monitoring prototype for long-duration missions, where a one-way signal delay of up to 22 minutes means crews cannot rely on real-time support from the ground. It compares each astronaut’s measurements with their own preflight baseline, explains in plain language why a reading was flagged, and links every finding to the NASA standard or study behind it. Cabin CO₂ and career radiation dose are checked against NASA reference limits. The app also includes cognitive assessments re-created from NASA’s Cognition battery and WinSCAT, guided exercise countermeasures with NASA demonstration footage, a daily briefing, and a crew view that shares status without exposing private measurements. It runs fully offline in a browser, with no ground connection. ASTRAMED matters because a crew on the way to Mars must notice and understand health changes early and on their own. All data is synthetic; it supports decisions and does not diagnose.
details:
ASTRAMED is a health monitoring system for astronauts on long missions, and it runs in a browser. It has four parts.

My Health compares each astronaut’s readings (reaction time, sleep, heart rate, blood pressure, oxygen saturation, activity and strength) with their own preflight baseline. The app marks a reading for review when it moves 15 to 20% from baseline and confirms it after three consecutive days. It checks cabin CO₂ and career radiation dose against NASA reference limits and alerts immediately if one is exceeded.

Every flag comes with an explanation: what was observed, the rule that triggered it, the NASA source behind it, and one next step.

Countermeasures has cognitive assessments re-created from NASA’s Cognition battery (Digit-Symbol Substitution, Fractal 2-Back, Visual Object Learning) and WinSCAT, plus guided exercise sessions with NASA demonstration footage.

Crew is a shared view of status and check-ins. It keeps individual measurements private and includes an option to report to the ground.

Benefits and intended impact

On a Mars transit, a one-way signal delay of up to 22 minutes rules out real-time medical support. We designed ASTRAMED so a tired crew member can understand a health change and act on it without the ground. We want crews to catch gradual changes earlier, such as sleep loss affecting reaction time, and to depend less on Earth.

Tools and technologies

We built the app with React 19, TypeScript, Vite, Tailwind CSS, Recharts and Lucide icons. We test with Vitest and Playwright, check code quality with ESLint, and use GitHub Actions to verify each change and publish to GitHub Pages. A service worker lets the app run fully offline, so it needs no special hardware. We used AI coding assistance and disclose it in the repository.

Creativity

The interface adapts to the mission environment (Mars transit, orbit, lunar surface, Earth) while status colours and limits never change. We wrote findings as explanations instead of alarms, and each one can be traced to its evidence.

Factors we considered

We wanted to be honest about limits. All data is synthetic, the thresholds are prototype choices, and the cognitive tests are unvalidated re-creations. The app says so wherever it matters. For privacy, crewmates see each other’s status and never the measurements. To cut false alarms, a single deviation only asks for a repeat measurement. For accessibility, the app has keyboard controls, captions and reduced-motion support. It supports decisions, and it does not diagnose or replace a flight surgeon.
